label: Configuring the machine
title: Agents gain from knowledge they cannot find, not from instructions
thesis: Most teams use a ready-made coding agent and shape the environment around it. Telling the agent how to work adds little, and less as models improve. What changes results is knowledge the agent cannot find for itself, such as unreleased interfaces, internal conventions and domain mappings. Teams also set limits on what it may touch. The work around the agent shifts from instructing it to supplying what it cannot discover and bounding what it can do.
currentPressure: Each model generation makes more of a team's hand-written instruction redundant: controlled tests find rules files and prescribed techniques add little or nothing, and a contract harness that rescued a cheap model only slowed a frontier one. The one test that supplied context the agent could not otherwise know found a large gain.

implications.statement: Engineers shape agent behaviour less by telling it how to work and more by supplying what it cannot know and limiting what it may touch.
Writing procedural instructions for agents becomes a perishable skill; curating organisational knowledge into a form agents can use becomes a lasting one.
Organisations standardise on a shared gateway and policy layer rather than on a single vendor's tool, changing what has to be agreed centrally.

evidence.note: named companies standardising the gateway rather than mandating one vendor's tool
systematic evaluation across 138 tasks finds repository context files often hinder rather than help

INFORMATION: Vercel evals on Next.js 16 APIs absent from training data; no docs 53%, on-demand docs skill 53% (unused in 56% of runs), 8KB docs index in AGENTS.md 100% on build/lint/test; vendor's own evals, model not stated

INFORMATION: Spotify Honk on Claude Code, no skills or MCP; context file adapted from the human migration guide left it guessing field mappings, explicit mapping tables fixed it; 240 migration PRs (qualitative before/after)

AUTHORITY plus scoped INFORMATION: Stripe maintains directory-scoped rules, a small default subset of a ~500-tool MCP server, and sandboxes with no production access around agents producing 1,300+ PRs/week; no comparison isolating any part

INFORMATION: Meta private monorepo, developer-written context files +6.4 pp solve rate on a basic harness, no benefit and slight harm on a harness with ~3x navigation tools; curated context redundant once the agent can find it
PROCEDURE: Boeckeler, five batches with and without TDD instructions, same agent and model (Sonnet 4.6); no quality or mutation-score difference for 2.96-8.5x the tokens

Dan Luu, 26 instructed conditions at ~80 trials each: naming a testing technique mostly did not produce it, defaults beat most instructed conditions, agents claimed methods they did not apply. Measured whether prompt-level configuration changes what the agent does

blinded test, 9 runs plus 82 attempts: full CLAUDE.md governance file scored 16.1/30 vs 16.3 with no guidance, two-sentence prompt 27.5; 0% compliance with behavioural rules. Measured whether written harness configuration improves outcomes; single author, small n

paired experiment, 10 runs per arm, 178 acceptance tests: contract harness (API contracts, examples, tests, mocks) took a cheap model from 3/10 to 10/10 passes at ~$0.27/run, but added ~7x cost for no gain on a frontier model. Harness value depends on the model

reachRationale: Named organisations now build the environment around ready-made agents as practice: Shopify and Ramp route agents through a shared gateway, Stripe keeps scoped rules, a curated tool set and sandboxes, Spotify and Vercel supply knowledge the model lacks. Independent experiments agree that instructions on how to work add little, while supplied knowledge helps only where the agent cannot find it, and not at all for a strong model on a simple task. That is spreading practice, not yet a settled expectation across the field, and limits are described rather than shown to change results.
whatWouldChangeThis: Controlled tests on work that depends on organisational knowledge find organisation-specific context no more effective than procedural instruction
Procedural instructions keep their measured value across successive model generations
Agents gather organisational context themselves, from code, tickets and documentation, well enough that curating it stops paying off
Organisations leave agents' tool access, permissions and sandboxing at vendor defaults, with no one deciding what agents may touch

developmentPaths.title: Context curation becomes a discipline
developmentPaths.description: Keeping organisational knowledge in a form agents can use develops its own owners, review and upkeep, in a way documentation never did.

developmentPaths.title: Standardise the gateway
developmentPaths.description: Organisations converge on a shared access and policy layer while leaving tool choice to teams.

developmentPaths.title: Capability absorbs the scaffolding
developmentPaths.description: Each model generation needs less of what teams write for it, and agents learn to gather organisational context themselves, until configuring their environment stops being work most teams do.

construct: What software teams put into the working environment of a packaged coding agent, and which parts of it change what the agent achieves while agent and model stay the same. Three kinds are distinguished: procedure — instructions on how to work, such as rules files, prescribed workflows and techniques, and checks the agent is made to run; information — what the agent cannot otherwise know, such as domain, architecture, conventions, design system, ownership and internal interfaces; and authority — what it may touch, such as tool and MCP access, permissions, sandboxes, gateways and policy layers. The construct also covers whether each kind's effect holds, shrinks or grows across model generations, and who designs, maintains and owns the environment. Not the harness inside the agent product (control loop, tool schemas, retry logic), including teams assembling their own agent from an SDK, except for the instruction, access and workflow elements any team configures. Not model benchmarks or releases, or agent adoption rates. Not the spread in delivery outcomes between teams with the same tooling, the acceptance suite as the definition of done, or how AI-generated changes are assured before merge — those belong to neighbouring phenomena.
